161: Hill continues emphasizing the importance of keeping one's mouth closed. If you talk more than you listen, you deprive yourself of useful knowledge and disclose your PLANS to people who may delight in defeating you out of envy. Every time you open your mouth before someone knowledgeable, you display your exact stock of knowledge or lack of it—genuine wisdom is conspicuous through modesty and silence. Everyone you associate with is seeking money; talking too freely about plans may result in someone beating you to your goal. He advises: 'TELL THE WORLD WHAT YOU INTEND TO DO, BUT FIRST SHOW IT'—deeds, not words, count most. Under 'Freedom or Death on a Decision,' Hill states the value of decisions depends upon the courage required. The great decisions serving as civilization's foundation involved great risks, often meaning possible death. Lincoln's decision to issue the Emancipation Proclamation was rendered knowing it would turn thousands against him and cost thousands of lives on the battlefield—and ultimately cost Lincoln his own life. That required courage.
162: Hill cites Socrates' decision to drink poison rather than compromise his beliefs—a decision of courage that turned time ahead a thousand years, giving unborn generations freedom of thought and speech. General Robert E. Lee's decision to side with the South required courage, knowing it might cost his life and others'. But the greatest decision for Americans was reached in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776, when 56 individuals signed a document knowing it would bring freedom or leave every one of them hanging from a gallows. We remember the date but few realize the courage required. We falsely imagine Washington was the Father of our Country and won our freedom, but Washington was an accessory after the fact—victory was ensured long before Cornwallis surrendered. Hill calls it a tragedy that history writers missed entirely the irresistible POWER that was the real cause of victory—the same POWER every individual must use to surmount life's difficulties and force life to pay the price asked.
163: Hill traces the events giving birth to this POWER. The story begins March 5, 1770, in Boston, when British soldiers patrolling streets were met with colonists' resentment—stones and epithets hurled until the commanding officer ordered 'Fix bayonets—Charge!' The battle resulted in death and injury, arousing such resentment that the Provincial Assembly called a meeting. Two members—John Hancock and Samuel Adams—spoke courageously, declaring that a move must be made to eject all British soldiers from Boston. Hill declares this DECISION in the minds of two individuals the beginning of American freedom. Adams was appointed to demand withdrawal from Governor Hutchinson; the request was granted, but the incident was not closed—it had caused a situation destined to change civilization's entire trend. Hill observes that great changes often begin in seemingly unimportant circumstances, usually as a DEFINITE DECISION in a relatively small number of minds. Few realize Hancock, Adams, and Richard Henry Lee of Virginia were the real Fathers of our Country. Lee became important because he and Adams corresponded frequently, sharing fears and hopes. Adams conceived the idea that mutual exchange of letters among the 13 colonies could coordinate effort.
164: In March 1772, two years after the Boston clash, Adams presented to the Assembly a motion for a Correspondence Committee among the colonies 'for the purpose of friendly cooperation for the betterment of the Colonies of British America.' Hill marks this as the beginning of the organization of far-flung POWER destined to give freedom. The Master Mind had already been organized—Adams, Lee, and Hancock. He quotes Matthew 18:19: 'If two of you agree upon the earth concerning anything for which you ask, it will come to you from My Father.' The Committee of Correspondence provided the way for increasing the Master Mind's power by adding people from all colonies—constituting the first ORGANIZED PLANNING of disgruntled colonists. In union there is strength. Citizens had waged disorganized warfare against British soldiers, but nothing was accomplished because individual grievances weren't consolidated under one Master Mind. Meanwhile, the British were also planning, with money and organized soldiery behind them. The Crown appointed Brig. General Thomas Gage to supplant Hutchinson as Governor. Gage sent Colonel Fenton to call on Adams to stop his opposition through fear and bribery.
165: Colonel Fenton conveyed Governor Gage's message: the Governor was empowered to confer satisfactory benefits if Adams would cease opposition. Fenton warned that Adams' conduct made him liable to penalties of an Act of Henry VIII, by which persons could be sent to England for trial for treason. But by changing his political course, Adams would receive great personal advantages and make peace with the King. Adams faced two DECISIONS: cease opposition and receive bribes, or CONTINUE AND RUN THE RISK OF BEING HANGED. Adams insisted on Fenton's word of honor to deliver the answer exactly. Adams replied: 'Tell Governor Gage that I trust I have long since made my peace with the King of Kings. No personal consideration shall induce me to abandon the righteous cause of my Country. And TELL GOVERNOR GAGE IT IS THE ADVICE OF SAMUEL ADAMS TO HIM, no longer to insult the feelings of an exasperated people.' When Gage received this caustic reply, he flew into a rage and issued a proclamation offering pardon to all who laid down arms, EXCEPTING Samuel Adams and John Hancock, whose offenses were too flagitious for any consideration but condign punishment.
166: Adams and Hancock were 'on the spot!' The threat forced them to reach another dangerous DECISION. They called a secret meeting of staunchest followers—the Master Mind began taking on momentum. Adams locked the door, placed the key in his pocket, and informed all present that a Congress of Colonists must be organized and NO ONE SHOULD LEAVE THE ROOM UNTIL THE DECISION FOR SUCH A CONGRESS HAD BEEN REACHED. Great excitement followed; some weighed consequences (Old Man Fear), others doubted the wisdom of defying the Crown. But Hancock and Adams were immune to fear, blind to failure. Through their influence, the others agreed that through the Correspondence Committee, arrangements should be made for the First Continental Congress in Philadelphia on September 5, 1774. Hill calls this date more important than July 4, 1776—without the decision to hold a Congress, there could have been no Declaration of Independence. Before the Congress met, Thomas Jefferson of Virginia was publishing his 'Summary View of the Rights of British America,' with a relationship as strained with Lord Dunmore as Hancock and Adams had with their Governor. Jefferson was informed he was subject to prosecution for high treason. Patrick Henry boldly declared: 'If this be treason, then make the most of it.'
167: Hill describes how these men—without power, authority, military strength, or money—sat in solemn consideration of the colonies' destiny from the First Continental Congress through intervals over two years until June 7, 1776, when Richard Henry Lee arose and made his astounding motion: 'Gentlemen, I make the motion that these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be free and independent states, that they be absolved from all allegiance to the British Crown, and that all political connection between them and the state of Great Britain is, and ought to be, totally dissolved.' After days of fervent discussion, Lee lost patience and declared: 'Why then, Sir, do we longer delay? Let this happy day give birth to an American Republic. Let her arise, not to devastate and to conquer, but to reestablish the reign of peace and of law.' Before the motion was voted upon, Lee was called back to Virginia due to family illness, placing his cause in Thomas Jefferson's hands. Hancock appointed Jefferson chairman of a committee to draft a Declaration of Independence. The committee labored long on a document that would mean everyone who signed it would be signing his own death warrant if the colonies lost. On July 4, 1776, Jefferson fearlessly read the most momentous DECISION ever placed upon paper.
168: When Jefferson finished, the document was voted upon, accepted, and signed by 56 representatives, every one staking his life on the DECISION. By that DECISION came into existence a nation destined to bring people the privilege of making DECISIONS. By decisions made in a similar spirit of FAITH can people solve personal problems and win high estates of material and spiritual wealth. Hill urges readers to analyze the events leading to the Declaration and be convinced that this nation was born of a DECISION created by a Master Mind of 56 persons. Their DECISION ensured Washington's armies' success because the spirit was in every soldier's heart—a spiritual power recognizing no such thing as FAILURE. The POWER that gave this nation freedom is the same power every individual must use to become self-determining, made up of the 13 principles in this book. At least six are detectable in the Declaration story: DESIRE, DECISION, FAITH, PERSISTENCE, THE MASTER MIND, and ORGANIZED PLANNING. Hill reminds readers that thought backed by strong DESIRE tends to transmute into its physical equivalent. The story contains no miracle—only the eternal laws of Nature, available to every person with FAITH and COURAGE. They may bring freedom to a nation, accumulate riches, or accomplish any worthwhile goal.
169: Hill states that those who reach DECISIONS promptly and definitely know what they want and generally get it. Leaders in every walk of life DECIDE quickly and firmly—that's the major reason they are leaders. The world makes room for those whose words and actions show they know where they're going. INDECISION is a habit beginning in youth, taking on permanency through grade school, high school, and college without DEFINITENESS OF PURPOSE. The major weakness of all educational systems is that they neither teach nor encourage the habit of DEFINITE DECISION. Hill suggests no college should enroll a student who hasn't declared a major purpose, and every grade school student should be trained in the HABIT OF DECISION. The habit of INDECISION goes with students into occupations—generally, young people take the first position found because they fell into the habit. Ninety-eight of every 100 wage earners are in their positions because they lacked DEFINITENESS OF DECISION to PLAN A DEFINITE POSITION. DEFINITENESS OF DECISION always requires courage. The 56 signers staked their lives; individuals who decide to procure a particular job stake their ECONOMIC FREEDOM. Financial independence and riches are not within reach of those who neglect to EXPECT, PLAN, and DEMAND these things.
170: Hill concludes Chapter 7 by reminding readers that Chapter 6 gave complete instructions for marketing personal services and choosing an employer and job. These instructions will be of no value UNLESS YOU DEFINITELY DECIDE to organize them into a plan of action and pursue that plan with PERSISTENCE—the Eighth Step to Riches.
